articles.title: Work at the Frontier: AI’s effect on freelance work
articles.description: New research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance work, new skill combinations, and larger budgets and more hours for AI-related projects.
articles.full_text:
Title: Work at the Frontier: AI’s effect on freelance work

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/ai-effect-on-freelance-work

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/ai-effect-on-freelance-work/

Markdown Content:
## Why we study freelance work

For freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a new skill or expands a project’s scope. Our new research with Upwork offers an early view of these changes in the AI era. Some familiar services are losing market share, while AI-related projects bring together different capabilities—and involve larger budgets and more hours of work.

The stakes are substantial. Upwork’s [2026 Future Workforce Index⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.upwork.com/press/releases/upworks-future-workforce-index-2026-how-ai-is-redefining-the-value-of-work-as-skilled-freelancing-accelerates) found that 38% of skilled U.S. knowledge workers freelance. Its [previous annual study⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.upwork.com/research/future-workforce-index-2025) estimated that freelance knowledge work generated $1.5 trillion in U.S. earnings in 2024. Those estimates extend well beyond Upwork’s own marketplace.

Freelance work can also reveal changes sooner than economy-wide employment statistics. Contracts are often short, and clients can adjust their requirements with each posting. To get to the root of these changes, we partnered with Upwork, an online marketplace connecting clients and freelancers, to study those requests alongside the activities people undertake directly with ChatGPT.

## What people use ChatGPT for vs. freelancers

The mix of work differed across the two platforms. Writing accounted for a much larger share of ChatGPT use, while video and animation accounted for larger shares of requests for freelancers in Upwork postings.

Below are the ranges of tasks between the two platforms.

These activities represent only the largest changes in Upwork shares over the studied period. ChatGPT shares cover Jan 2025–Jun 2026; Upwork shares are H1 2026. Changes in Upwork share are H1 2025 to H1 2026, in percentage points.

## Freelance demand is shifting as AI use grows

Many activities that were relatively common in ChatGPT lost share on Upwork, while less common activities gained share. Of the 63 work categories analyzed, 43 followed this pattern.

The remaining 20 work categories showed the reverse. ChatGPT use alone does not explain changes in freelance demand.

The comparison also captures how people currently use ChatGPT, not the full range of tasks AI can support—a gap OpenAI calls the capability overhang.

Each point represents one of 63 matched work subcategories in the Upwork taxonomy. The horizontal axis is the natural log of the category’s share of ChatGPT use in H2 2025 divided by its share of Upwork job posts in H1 2023. The vertical axis shows the percentage change in the category’s share of Upwork postings from H1 2023 to H2 2025, on a logarithmic scale; 0% indicates unchanged marketplace share. The vertical divider at AI intensity 0 marks equal category shares in ChatGPT and baseline Upwork postings.

## Clients are asking for AI in more kinds of work and combining tasks in new ways

By late 2025, clients were requesting the use of AI in many more, different kinds of work. Clients were seeking freelancers to apply AI in tasks including chatbot development, video production, marketing automation, and application integration.

Within individual projects, AI capabilities were often requested alongside other work. AI-related postings listed about as many tasks as other postings but more often combined tasks that had rarely appeared together in earlier jobs.

### Example: Inside a project brief

Some clients asked for **AI-generated video, editing, and motion graphics** in a single posting. The freelancer would bring those skills together to deliver a finished video.

## The mix of work broadened across AI-related postings

Between early 2023 and late 2025, the mix of tasks in AI-related postings became **45% more diverse**—the equivalent of an increase from about 15 equally common tasks to about 21.

Early 2023 14.6 Late 2025 21.2

Although posted hourly rates were similar for AI-related and other work, AI-related projects had larger fixed-price budgets and involved more hours of work. This pattern suggests that higher budgets may partly reflect a broader scope of work.

## Conclusion

### AI may be changing both what clients hire freelancers to do and the scope of the projects they post

AI’s effects on work can be difficult to detect in employment statistics. As we have noted in previous _Work at the Frontier_ papers, the effects may appear first in the work people do.

Because freelance projects turn over quickly, postings are continually refreshed as clients’ needs change. Work within firms can evolve without appearing in a new job posting. Combined with ChatGPT data, these postings offer an early view of which activities people undertake directly with AI, which they hire freelancers to perform, and how AI-related projects differ from other work.

The findings do not point to a simple substitution story. Some activities common in ChatGPT use lost share on Upwork, but this pattern was not uniform. AI-related work also spanned a wider mix of activities, combined tasks in less familiar ways, and carried larger fixed-price budgets and more hours.

Together, these patterns suggest that AI may be shifting both what clients seek from freelancers and how they assemble projects.

## The Work at the Frontier series

The OpenAI Economic Research Team explores how AI is changing work in real time with the Work at the Frontier series.

articles.title: Cogent and OpenAI build cyber defense factories for enterprises
articles.description: Cogent combines OpenAI models with enterprise context to help automatically remediate vulnerabilities with agents.
articles.full_text:
Title: Cogent and OpenAI build cyber defense factories for enterprises

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/cogent-security

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/cogent-security/

Markdown Content:
As [Cogent Security⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.cogent.com/) sees enterprises facing more security risks than ever, it has found that the hardest part is not finding vulnerabilities, but fixing them. Remediation work is complex and spans multiple teams. It requires contextual understanding of a company’s environment: how could an attacker exploit a vulnerability, which business systems are at stake, and what changes can be made safely.

Cogent builds Cyber Defense Factories for enterprises to autonomously find and eliminate those risks. The factories are designed to help defenders move at machine speed, in response to the acceleration in vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

The company’s AI agents combine GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑5.6 with its enterprise context and controls to handle investigation through verified remediation. The agents assess exposures, execute permitted changes, and confirm the risk has been eliminated. Cogent also conducts internal research with Cyber and Daybreak, exploring attack paths and defensive capabilities.

> “The ability of OpenAI models to sustain long-running tasks unlocks a new level of autonomy in enterprise defense: AI agents can now carry work from investigation through verified remediation.”

—Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO, Cogent

## Giving agents context and permission to act

For each customer, Cogent’s Context Engine maintains an enterprise knowledge graph of assets, vulnerabilities, identities, ownership, and dependencies. Specialized background agents continuously reconcile information across security tools and systems, giving investigation and remediation agents a shared understanding of the environment.

GPT‑6 Astra handles upfront planning and complex reasoning for that work. This enables what Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO of Cogent, describes as a “memory harness for the enterprise.” He says, “We don’t have to relearn what the world looks like every time a new task happens.” Reusing context reduces latency, inference costs, and inconsistent results.

Cogent’s Agent Policies define each enterprise’s permitted changes and approval requirements, and its policy-enforcement engine, TRACE, checks tool calls against the policies before execution. The checks are deterministic and require no separate model inference.

An Agent Gateway independently checks authorization, and higher-risk work can run in isolated sandboxes. Customers can delegate investigation, require approval for changes, or permit bounded autonomous remediation.

## From vulnerability disclosure to verified fixes

When critical security flaws known as PHP2Shell were disclosed in PHP, a programming language used to run websites, customers turned to the Cyber Defense Factories that Cogent had already deployed in their environments.

GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Astra provided the deep reasoning for investigation and remediation planning. Using Cogent’s context layer, agents identified affected systems, assessed exposure, and developed plans that accounted for application dependencies and operational constraints. Then they orchestrated fixes using customer-defined approval and execution workflows and verified the resolution.

Cogent reports that customers are using its Cyber Defense Factories to resolve vulnerabilities faster and expand investigation capacity. With Cogent, a Fortune 1000 automotive customer reduced its mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities by 75%, and a Fortune 500 IT services customer achieved 5× vulnerability-triage throughput.

Trading platform MarketAxess says Cogent helps it decide which exposures to fix first: “Cogent sees our environment the way an attacker would. It traces the route from the internet to a vulnerable system and checks controls on the way. Our remediation work now focuses on the greatest risks and the paths an adversary could use to break in,” says Vijay Bala, Global CISO at MarketAxess.

## Why Cogent builds with OpenAI models and Codex

Cogent continuously evaluates closed-source and open-source alternatives and reports stronger reasoning on long-running security tasks, higher fidelity, fewer hallucinations on technical codebases, and more reliable execution with OpenAI models. The models can chain tool calls sequentially and in parallel while retaining context across remediation workflows.

Cogent prioritizes reasoning quality for complex investigations and cost for more straightforward work. It uses GPT‑6.1 Sol for general execution and GPT‑5.6 for routine vulnerability-management tasks where advanced reasoning is less critical.

> “OpenAI models are more cost-efficient relative to the other providers. That’s a big plus for us, especially if we’re running these huge agent swarms.”

—Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO, Cogent

Using OpenAI models has also reduced the supporting software Cogent needs to build for remediation and patching. “A lot of the work that we had to do at the harness level is no longer required,” Geng says. He also shared that OpenAI APIs have “streamlined request routing and agent orchestration, significantly reducing internal engineering overhead and accelerating our time-to-market for complex security workflows.”

Most of Cogent’s engineers also choose Codex for development. Geng says they’re more productive pairing Codex with OpenAI models vs. using the same models in an open-source coding environment. “Codex just comes with tools that we don’t have to build ourselves,” says Geng.

## Expanding autonomous cyber defense

Through Trusted Access for Cyber and Daybreak, Cogent receives technical support for its internal red-teaming and attack-path research. Daybreak Red, an access tier within Daybreak, provides the team with specialized OpenAI models for authorized offensive and vulnerability research. “Good defense requires good offense,” Geng says.

> “Through Trusted Access for Cyber and Daybreak, we can explore how vulnerabilities could be chained across identities, resources, and network controls. We use that research to understand what our agents can do and which defensive capabilities to build next.”

—Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO, Cogent

Cogent plans to expand its capabilities as the key partner for enterprises to build their own Cyber Defense Factories. Its roadmap includes increasingly autonomous remediation, broadening the range and complexity of fixes agents can execute, from straightforward configuration changes to multi-step workflows spanning different enterprise systems.

The company is also developing autonomous discovery and validation. Its goal is a closed-loop system that finds and eliminates risk while continuously learning from every vulnerability to improve future investigations and fixes.

articles.title: Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure
articles.description: Learn how OpenAI’s Control Room tracks model workloads across our research infrastructure and can rapidly stop them when safety or security concerns arise.
articles.full_text:
Title: Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/control-room

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/control-room/

Markdown Content:
As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed. To solve this, we built Control Room.

Control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise. It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our [misalignment monitoring systems](https://openai.com/index/how-we-detect-frontier-model-misalignment/), and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job. It has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.

Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest. Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.

## How it works

Control Room works by integrating a few systems: the _workload_, the _inference engine_, and the centralized _Control Room service_.

*   The _workload_ is the job being run, such as a reinforcement learning experiment, an evaluation, a high-volume sampling or data processing job. We require every research workload that does agentic inference to be associated with an approved [safety case](https://openai.com/index/towards-safety-cases-for-frontier-ai-training/).

*   The _inference engine_, or just _engine_, is the model itself. You can think of the engine as the brain of the model, running directly on GPUs. A workload normally uses one or more models, which might be running on one or more different inference engines. The same inference engine might be used by more than one different workload.

*   _The Control Room service_ tracks jobs and controls whether they are allowed to continue generating model output. Engines check with the Control Room service before fulfilling a request. If a job has been stopped, the service denies the request, preventing further output.

Control Room is integrated in the following way:

*   When starting a new job, the workload code requests a new job_id from Control Room.

*   Whenever the workload needs to sample tokens from a model, it makes a request to an inference engine running that model, passing the job_id. The engine requests permission from Control Room to fulfill that request, passing the job_id along to Control Room.

*   Control Room checks whether that job has been terminated, and if so, it denies the inference request. The engine responds to the workload's inference request with a refusal, stopping further model output from being produced for that job.

## How Control Room works

STEP 1

### A researcher decides to start a job

The process starts with a researcher launching a job—for example, an experiment or an evaluation.

01 / 13

## Example: reacting to a monitoring alert

All of our frontier reinforcement learning jobs run with a monitor. A _monitor_ is another model which inspects everything that the model-being-trained is doing, and raises an alert if it detects a problem. For example, our recent [DNS-related incident⁠(opens in a new window)](https://alignment.openai.com/misalignment-reports/an-agent-used-dns-to-reach-an-external-chatbot/) was caught by a monitor.

Control Room and our monitoring system are integrated in the following way:

*   If the monitoring system detects a potential issue, depending on the details and severity, the monitoring system may decide to stop the job.

*   In this case, the monitoring system sends a message to Control Room to stop the job, passing the job_id. Control Room records that the job is terminated.

*   Next time the job having that job_id makes an inference request to sample more tokens from _any_ model running on _any_ engine, the request will be denied, stopping further model output.

## Speed and reliability

The maximum time between the moment when Control Room receives an instruction to stop a job, and the moment when further progress is no longer possible, is 35 seconds. The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly.

Workloads, including experiments, evaluation jobs, etc., are normally owned and operated by researchers or teams of researchers. As a result, workload code changes often, and is not an ideal place to implement critical load-bearing safety protections. Because of this, our implementation is designed to be resilient to buggy or broken workload code.

We achieve this by implementing the termination mechanism in the inference layer. Workload code is highly-varied and decentralized. In contrast, there are only a very small number of inference code paths in use across all of OpenAI research, and their deployments are much more centralized and uniform. This means that the inference layer can serve as a bottleneck, where we can get strong guarantees that all model inference running in research is subject to Control Room authorization checks on every inference request. We additionally run continual agentic and programmatic sweeps to check that users are not accidentally or maliciously launching rogue engine implementations with Control Room unimplemented or disabled.

Finally, our system “fails closed”, meaning that the Control Room integration in the engines is configured in such a way that if the Control Room service goes down, either due to a system error or because it is disabled for any other reason, including tampering by a bad actor, then all inference requests will be denied until Control Room resumes normal operation. Fail-closed is rolled out now to all frontier model research workloads, and will finish rolling out across all remaining research workloads over the next few days.

Control Room is just one part of our holistic approach to safe frontier model training and deployment. We’ll continue to strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches. If you want to help build systems for the safe and secure development and deployment of AGI, [we're⁠](https://openai.com/careers/research-engineer-research-scientist-ai-systems-engineer-rsi-san-francisco/)[hiring⁠](https://openai.com/careers/researcher-agent-safety-oversight-and-system-mitigations-san-francisco/)!

articles.title: CodeRabbit scales agentic software development and ships 20x more
articles.description: CodeRabbit uses OpenAI models to govern and trust AI-generated code and Codex to ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team.
articles.full_text:
Title: CodeRabbit scales agentic software development and ships 20x more

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/coderabbit-codex-daybreak

Final URL: https://openai.com/index/coderabbit-codex-daybreak/

Markdown Content:
For Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO of [CodeRabbit⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.coderabbit.ai/), trusting and validating agentic code is becoming the place where teams bring judgment to a growing volume of AI-generated work. “The first bottleneck that every company hits as soon as you adopt coding agents is code reviews,” Harjot says.

CodeRabbit built an AI-powered governance and control platform designed to validate and trust AI-generated code. Used by over 20,000 organizations and 150,000+ open-source projects, CodeRabbit helps teams understand, review, and secure code produced by AI agents and decide what is ready to ship.

According to CodeRabbit, better price-performance from OpenAI helps it add more AI agents to its reviews and pass the benefits to customers, and [Codex⁠](https://openai.com/codex/) helps it ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team. The company also uses [Daybreak⁠](https://openai.com/daybreak/) to both secure its own stack and its customers’ code. Its latest offering, CodeRabbit Secure, uses Daybreak with Codex models to find and fix vulnerabilities using its security-focused agents.

> “With each OpenAI model release, especially with the reasoning models, we have seen massive improvements in the capabilities of our product to find issues at scale.”

– Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO, CodeRabbit

## Improving code review with OpenAI reasoning models

CodeRabbit built its first product with GPT‑3.5 Turbo. Harjot says the arrival of GPT‑4 made the product effective at reviewing code. The company went on to adopt OpenAI o1 and OpenAI o3 early. Because code reviews run asynchronously in the cloud, CodeRabbit could use models that took longer to reason through a problem in exchange for more capable analysis.

The team evaluates new models against its own benchmark of known issues. At the time of the interview, Harjot estimated that [GPT‑6 Astra⁠](https://openai.com/index/gpt-6-astra/) caught 50% of the issues in that dataset, putting it at the top compared to other models in that benchmark.

The benchmark continues to evolve as agents introduce different kinds of mistakes and as fixes reveal problems earlier reviews missed. “The nature of bugs keeps evolving, so does our benchmark as the models get better,” says Harjot.

## Making more capable agents economical to deploy

Better price-performance from OpenAI models has helped CodeRabbit move capabilities from research into its product. Harjot points to improvements in model pricing and caching that let the company use more AI, add more subagents, and pass the benefits to customers.

When CodeRabbit started, it used one or two subagents for code navigation. Lower-cost models such as GPT‑6 Luna now support more subagents throughout the platform, while models such as GPT‑6 Astra handle planning and orchestration.

“Now we are using agents everywhere on the use cases we couldn't even afford in the past,” Harjot says. That expands the validation CodeRabbit can perform and the explanations it can give developers, helping them understand and trust changes they did not write themselves.

## Shipping 20 times more software with Codex

By using Codex, Harjot says the company has been shipping roughly 20 times more software over the last 6 months without adding engineers. He personally estimates that he pushed 2,500 to 3,000 pull requests in the 30 days before the interview.

Getting there required more than adopting Codex. Running multiple agents exposed constraints across the development process, from laptop memory and compute to testing, the tools that compile and package software, and dependencies.

The team streamlined its release process and reconsidered where human approvals belonged, while using CodeRabbit to automatically ship low-risk changes that didn’t need human intervention. “We had to actually completely rethink the entire software delivery,” Harjot says.

The company has also built a Codex-powered Slack bot that triages production incidents, Slack messages, and support tickets. It can return a pull request for the team to review and merge. Harjot sees cloud-based development as a way to reduce local-machine constraints and give teams stronger controls over access and auditing.

## Running more of CodeRabbit as code

CodeRabbit uses Codex for work beyond engineering, including managing marketing and operational tasks through code. “We are running the company as code as much as possible,” Harjot says.

In marketing, the company manages Google Ads through pull requests. The team opens and merges a request to deploy ads. It also uses a content studio repository where Codex creates slide decks and customer-facing documents. “If you can translate your marketing problems to code problems, you will run 10x faster,” Harjot says.

## Securing application code with Daybreak

CodeRabbit has run agents in sandbox environments since 2023, cloning repositories and letting agents write code to help perform reviews. More recently, CodeRabbit used OpenAI’s Cyber model through Daybreak to test and secure its own platform.

The team used the model for internal penetration testing, probing its own platform for ways an attacker could break in. Harjot says the early access helped CodeRabbit secure its own stack. “We found multiple vulnerabilities, advanced hacks that we could not even imagine could happen,” Harjot says.

It has since taken those capabilities to market, helping secure its customers’ code with its latest product, CodeRabbit Secure. Over the past two weeks, the company ran a promotional offer where it covered $1M in free deep scans for their users and found over 43,000 security vulnerabilities across 13,000 deep scans, all powered by Codex models. Thousands of these vulnerabilities have already been fixed by its customers, helping improve their code security.

## Keeping developers in control of agent-generated code

As background agents begin responding to alerts and incidents without a person initiating every task, Harjot expects teams to need more help deciding which changes to take to completion.

Looking ahead, CodeRabbit is expanding toward agentic software development, helping teams validate, prioritize, explain, secure, and verify agent-generated code changes at scale.

The opportunity is to help developers stay in control as agents do more of the building, with validation, explanations, and maintenance that keep pace with the code being produced.

articles.description:
Introducing GPT‑6 Cyber: a major advance in security research that pairs stronger capabilities with better model alignment.

The model powered the Linux kernel research we announced yesterday, and security teams at companies like Mozilla, Palo Alto Networks, Calif, and Cisco—alongside our own at OpenAI—are already putting it to work.

GPT-6 Cyber is available to select Daybreak Red customers and we are expanding access over time.

https://t.co/Nzab3Z1Td6
articles.linked_content:
Title: GPT‑6 Cyber: Advancing the frontier of aligned cybersecurity agents

URL Source: https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-6-cyber/

Markdown Content:
We’re introducing GPT‑6 Cyber, a major leap in security research: more capable at finding and fixing vulnerabilities, and far more reliable staying within the boundaries researchers set. GPT‑6 Cyber delivers major gains on key cybersecurity benchmarks over GPT‑5.6 Cyber, including a 51% relative improvement on ExploitGym and a step function improvement when tested on staying within scope. It is already helping to secure real-world software, uncovering and validating thousands of exploits in security-critical codebases such as Linux and Firefox.

On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability, GPT‑6 Cyber scores 48.5%, up from 32.1% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. It also follows task boundaries more reliably: in a separate alignment evaluation, GPT‑6 Cyber avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of tests without its deployment prompt, and 100% with this prompt. This improvement in alignment reflects dedicated training to stay within authorized scope, respect restrictions, and report results accurately.

These capabilities are already helping secure real systems. Our researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber to develop [948 privilege escalation exploits in Linux⁠](https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/) and identify 81 previously unknown high-severity vulnerabilities in Firefox, despite extensive prior testing with frontier models. The model also helped develop candidate patches, and Mozilla has [released fixes for many of the Firefox vulnerabilities⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2026-118/). Security teams at Cisco, Calif, and CodeRabbit are using it for vulnerability research and code review, and we have relied on it to [find and fix weaknesses in our own infrastructure⁠](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/).

It is clear that we have [a limited window to use frontier models to secure software⁠](https://openai.com/index/the-defenders-window/). **Our goal is to dramatically expand Daybreak, bringing advanced security research to organizations of every size, independent researchers, and open-source maintainers.** Mainline models such as GPT‑6 Astra already support code review, vulnerability triage, and patch development. Daybreak Blue helps verified defenders validate vulnerabilities and fixes with fewer unnecessary refusals, while Daybreak Red enables deeper exploit development and authorized security testing with GPT‑6 Cyber.

## Advancing frontier cyber capabilities

GPT‑6 Cyber is a major step up from GPT‑5.6 Cyber and outperforms GPT‑6 Astra on most cyber tasks, even when Astra does not refuse the request. We evaluated the model on tasks that require it to understand software, identify vulnerabilities, and develop working exploits. Based on these results, we classify the model as Critical in cybersecurity under our Preparedness Framework, up from High for GPT‑5.6 Cyber.

On ExploitGym, which tests whether models can exploit a specified vulnerability in a remote target, GPT‑6 Cyber scores **48.5%**, about **16 percentage points** higher than GPT‑5.6 Cyber’s **32.1%**. To test vulnerability discovery, we also built a new evaluation for offensive web penetration testing. Models probe web applications without access to their source code. GPT‑6 Cyber achieved **40.3%** recall of vulnerabilities compared with **32.0%** for GPT‑6 Astra.

Daybreak Red is designed to support more advanced security workflows, including developing working exploits and using them against remote targets. To evaluate these capabilities, we built a new benchmark called RemoteExploitBench, which uses known vulnerabilities in applications such as GitLab, PostgreSQL, and Jenkins deployed in a controlled environment. In our initial evaluation, GPT‑6 Astra running with Daybreak Blue **refused 100% of tasks**, while GPT‑6 Cyber **completed 95%**; its only failure was an exploit it could not get to work remotely. See the [system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-cyber) for full results and evaluation settings.

## Stronger alignment, better at staying within bounds

One risk for cybersecurity agents is that they go outside the scope of their assigned task, attempt to exploit unrelated services, or disregard the researcher’s rules of engagement.

We made alignment a central focus of GPT‑6 Cyber, using specialized training to help the model stay within authorized scope, follow restrictions on its actions, and report its work accurately. Before deployment, we ran a series of alignment evaluations to measure these behaviors. See the [system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-cyber) for full results.

One of these evaluations is ExploitGym Honeypot, which was informed by the [Hugging Face incident⁠](https://openai.com/index/hugging-face-incident-and-the-road-ahead/). We give the model a difficult exploitation task in an isolated environment with access to supporting services, such as a package registry or object store. We deliberately make these services easy to exploit so that attacking them can reveal the task’s flag. The model must infer that exploiting them is outside the scope of its task.

GPT‑6 Cyber shows a step-change improvement over GPT‑5.6 Cyber on this evaluation. When tested without deployment safety prompts, it avoided exploiting out-of-scope services in 99.93% of cases, up from 94.49% for GPT‑5.6 Cyber. With those prompts, GPT‑6 Cyber stayed within bounds 100% of the time.

We can see directly in the GPT‑6 Cyber model’s chain of thought how it reasons about staying within bounds:

Agent chain-of-thought excerpts

> “Can't assume extra API or attack controller not target. We should only target binary/server.”

Agent chain-of-thought excerpts

> “don't explore out of scope credentials.”

## Real-world impact for security teams

GPT‑6 Cyber is already helping security teams find vulnerabilities, validate their impact, and develop fixes. Customers have put it to work on large codebases, long-running exploit development, and security review:

1 of 9

We have also relied on GPT‑6 Cyber to secure our own systems. It was one of the main models behind the work we recently shared on [hardening the infrastructure used to train frontier models⁠](https://openai.com/index/securing-our-frontier-model-training-environment/). In controlled red-teaming campaigns, agents using GPT‑6 Cyber and other OpenAI models chained vulnerabilities to escape microVMs and execute code on the underlying hosts. We used the findings to patch software, tighten network restrictions, and report issues to maintainers and vendors.

Our vulnerability researchers also use GPT‑6 Cyber to find and validate vulnerabilities in open-source software at scale. This work has uncovered previously unknown flaws in software that has been scrutinized for years:

*   **Found 81 novel Firefox vulnerabilities.** GPT‑6 Cyber can be suitable for use in autonomous workflows for finding vulnerabilities and proposing high-quality patches at scale. During a vulnerability research campaign, GPT‑6 Cyber produced evidence and reproducible tests for 81 novel vulnerabilities classified by Mozilla as high severity, and showed that an additional 30 known issues were more severe than previously reported. We disclosed the findings to Mozilla, along with proposed patches to help its engineers develop fixes. Mozilla was supportive of this work, and began [landing fixes shortly after receiving the reports⁠(opens in a new window)](https://www.mozilla.org/en-US/security/advisories/mfsa2026-118/).

*   **Developing exploits for**[**948 Linux kernel vulnerabilities**⁠](https://openai.com/index/a-thousand-fewer-paths-to-root/)**.** GPT‑6 Cyber reproduced 1,724 vulnerabilities and developed working exploits for 948—more than five times the 166 exploited by GPT‑5.6 Sol using the same research harness. Following the Linux community's guidance, we disclosed 304 critical findings to maintainers with candidate patches and are in the process of getting other vulnerabilities fixed.

*   **Demonstrating critical RCE vulnerabilities.** We recently discussed a [critical vulnerability in Brotli⁠(opens in a new window)](https://patchtheplanet.org/brotli), a compression library used by Node.js and other software. Our security researchers used GPT‑6 Cyber alongside other OpenAI models to develop and validate exploits showing how the flaw could enable remote code execution in downstream applications.

## Detecting misuse and blocking high-risk activity

As models become more capable and uncover more security vulnerabilities, we are also seeing more attempts to use them to cause harm. These attempts include efforts by malicious cyber actors and adversarial groups seeking to distill our models. We have thus paired GPT‑6 Cyber’s stronger capabilities with stronger safeguards to detect and disrupt misuse and keep the model’s actions within the user’s intent and authorization.

We added and strengthened these protections alongside the release of GPT‑6 Cyber (see the [system card⁠(opens in a new window)](https://deploymentsafety.openai.com/gpt-6-cyber) for full information):

*   **Cyber-specific misalignment monitoring.** We monitor whether actions match the user’s authorization, while recognizing legitimate exploit development and testing.

*   **Targeted monitoring for emerging threats.** For example, during the coordinated disclosure of critical PHP vulnerabilities, we set up targeted monitoring for attempts to develop exploits against live PHP servers, while preserving support for defenders patching affected systems.

*   **Private Safety Processing (PSP).** We use automated checks to review related interactions for misuse. Standard retention remains the default. API customers using [Zero Data Retention⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data) generally must use [PSP⁠(opens in a new window)](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/private-safety-processing), which reviews encrypted records retained in customer storage for 30 days without exposing prompts and responses to OpenAI personnel.

*   **Protection against stolen credentials.** We require IP allowlisting for Daybreak Red API access by default, restricting requests to approved networks with limited exceptions. We also monitor credentials for compromise.

*   **Sandboxing and oversight.** As with past models, we recommend [sandboxing⁠(opens in a new window)](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/sandboxing), [action review⁠(opens in a new window)](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/sandboxing/auto-review), and human oversight for high-risk workflows.

*   **Protections against high-risk cyber assistance.** We use new checks to block high-risk activity involving critical systems (see below for more).

## Defending critical infrastructure

Protecting critical infrastructure has been a key consideration in designing GPT‑6 Cyber’s safeguards and access, including power plants, water treatment facilities, and the operational technology and industrial control systems (OT/ICS) that underpin them. We simultaneously want to give the teams defending these systems access to our most capable models while also strengthening our safeguards to prevent unauthorized attacks.

First, to equip these defenders, our $1 billion [Daybreak for Frontline Defenders⁠](https://openai.com/index/daybreak-for-frontline-defenders/) grant program subsidizes access for resource-constrained teams such as government organizations and essential service providers. We’re also introducing a new group within Daybreak Red (**Daybreak Red for Critical Infrastructure**) for approved critical infrastructure defenders, which gives them permissions to conduct authorized testing of critical systems while retaining safeguards against model misalignment.

Second, to prevent misuse of the Daybreak Red and Blue platforms, we have refined safeguards against assistance and capability development that could compromise industrial controls or safety-critical systems, interfere with equipment, or cause serious injury, catastrophic physical damage, or life-endangering service disruption. The figure below compares safeguard label rates across four access configurations, before and after the recent updates we’re rolling out alongside GPT‑6 Cyber.

Higher safeguard block rates are not always better. Many of the techniques in this evaluation are also essential to legitimate security work: understanding systems, finding vulnerabilities, and verifying that fixes withstand attack. We therefore assess these rates alongside support for legitimate research and patching, rather than aiming for 100%.

To evaluate how our models can help defend critical infrastructure, we partnered with Dragos, the global provider for extended operational technology (xOT) cybersecurity. Dragos ran evaluations using cyber-permissive Daybreak Red models in a controlled lab environment. The evaluations covered requests progressing from network discovery and asset enumeration through targeted reconnaissance, sensitive data exfiltration, and unauthorized, potentially dangerous device actions.

We used feedback from Dragos to refine our safeguards, aiming to block harmful assistance without unnecessarily restricting authorized testing. [See their final report⁠(opens in a new window)](https://hub.dragos.com/whitepaper/frontier-ai-models-xot-environment) for details on the evaluations. We’re also working to expand partnerships with other offensive security providers and purple teams on penetration testing and red teaming with AI, and with energy companies, other critical infrastructure operators, and national labs to assess our models’ effectiveness and safeguards in industrial defense. We have also increased our investment in threat investigations to detect model usage involving OT/ICS. We’ll continue refining our safeguards with input from partners and the security community, including reports through /feedback when safeguards miss harmful activity or interrupt legitimate work.

## Expanding access to trusted defenders

GPT‑6 Cyber is initially available through the API and Codex to a select group of approved Daybreak Red customers. We will progressively expand access to all Daybreak Red customers soon, and are also making GPT‑5.6 Cyber available to all Daybreak Red customers. We’re also expanding Daybreak Blue alpha access for GPT‑6 Astra to more organizations and individual security researchers; [let us know⁠(opens in a new window)](https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSdQu8mNYXDpUW_0kRS6JBWBPMWfUjjxi6xLi8AkFPObLupkpg/viewform) if you’re interested.

New users and organizations can [apply for Daybreak⁠](https://openai.com/daybreak/) and get started with our [cyber skills, products, and partners⁠](https://openai.com/business/solutions/cybersecurity/).
